messages.author: 89a4640ddc6e46d0
messages.subject: Random Effect for Gamme Inverse Scale Parameter
parts:
Hi,

I've developed a hierarchical model. The key elements are as follows
parameters{
real <lower=0> tau_l_s;
real l_s_pr
}
model{
tau_l_s ~ cauchy(0,0.8211569);
l_s_prior ~ normal(1.72656, 3.284628);
l_s ~ normal(l_s_prior, tau_l_s);
data ~ gamma (exp(l_s), some other parameter);

}
generated quantities{
real l_s_new;
real s_new;

l_s_new <- normal_rng(l_s_prior, tau_l_s);
s_new <- exp(l_s_new);

for (i in 1:Ntm){
perc_L_E_7[i]<-gamma_cdf(7, s_new, some_positive_paramter);
}
}


I am running 4 chains in parallel. In the early warm-up, I get errors that the inverse scale parameter for gamma is 0 or infinity. But this eventually stops. However, for one or 2 chains I get the error
Error : Error in function stan::prob::gamma_cdf(d): Scale parameter is 0, but must be > 0!
error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done

Then sampling for these chains stops.

Is there something I can do to prevent this? I'm guessing I get a large value for tau_l_s, and then sample a large negative number for l_s. Is there any way to allow the program to proceed through warm-up?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Random Effect for Gamme Inverse Scale Parameter
parts:
You can

a. provide reasonable initial values for tau_l_s and l_s_pr
by hand,

b. reduce the initial step size (epsilon),

c. increase the target acceptance rate (delta).

You could also figure out the range of the CDF and replace
out of range values with NaN in a conditional statement during
generated quantities.

In general, taking exp() transforms of unconstrained variables
is dangerous. In particular tau_l_s has a very fat tail with
the Cauchy and you are then sampling l_s with that scale, and
any value too high is going to overflow (don't know the exact
boundary).

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Random Effect for Gamme Inverse Scale Parameter
parts:
You only need something centered roughly where you know the answer
will be and not excluding reasonable values. And then maybe make it
a bit wider. The point is that if you're expecting values in the -2 to 2
range, you want to convey that in the prior rather than having a prior
that's uniform, say from -1000 to 1000.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Random Effect for Gamme Inverse Scale Parameter
parts:
> On Oct 29, 2014, at 10:39 AM, Markian Pahuta <mark....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> OK. But for a parameter constrained to >0, are there any papers describing a better way to do this?

Again, see the references to the papers by Andrew and collaborators
in the references. Some of them are for coefficients and some of them
are for variances/deviations/precisions.

> Gamma inverse scale parameter:
> I've tried using the cauchy, but I end up getting lots of draws of zero. Could I change the location to my expected value?

Yes, that's a good idea, too, if you know where it is. We
should probably not be using Cauchy(0,5) and the like for
scale parameters anyway --- I'd think Cauchy(1,5) would be better,
not that it's that much different. A weak prior like this may not
be able to overcome the data.
> I've been using the exp() approach described above, but I overflow the sampler.

You can use a gamma (not inverse gamma) on the scale and get
zero-avoiding behavior that doesn't pollute the estimates too much
Again, see the manual chapter and reference paper by Andrew and crew on zero-avoiding priors.

By overflow the sampler you mean it runs off to -infinity on the log
scale? Or do you just mean it runs to below -800 or so on the log
scale and thus exp(-800) underflows to 0?

- Bob

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Random Effect for Gamme Inverse Scale Parameter
parts:
Priors such as the lognormal cut off at 0 and are appropriate if you think the parameter can’t be very close to 0.  Priors such as the half-normal go all the way to 0 and are appropriate if you don’t want to rule out values very close to 0.
In general I don’t see any good reason to put a model on the inverse of a scale parameter.

On Oct 29, 2014, at 10:45 AM, Avraham Adler <avraha...@gmail.com> wrote:

If it's constrained to >1 the simple (and probably naïve) solutions are 1) sample from a distribution constrained to positive values (e.g. simple pareto) or 2) sample in log space and exponentiate.

On Wednesday, October 29, 2014 10:39:54 AM UTC-4, Markian Pahuta wrote:
OK. But for a parameter constrained to >0, are there any papers describing a better way to do this?
